extracted.intended_audience: federal judges, patent litigators, and counsel who draft or use jury instructions in patent trials
extracted.subtask_description: Model jury instructions and legal standards for patent litigation, covering invalidity doctrines (printed publications, prior invention, prior patents and applications, obviousness), enablement, written description, and damages. Intended to guide what juries should be told and what legal elements/burdens apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printed Publication
rubrics_metrics.description: [The Defendant] contends that claim ___ ... is invalid because the invention defined in that claim was described in a printed publication before [[§ 102(a) (AIA) Cutoff Date] ...]. That patent claim is invalid if a publication printed [[before the effective filing date] [before the date of invention by the applicant] [more than one year before the date of application in the United States]] was maintained in some tangible form ... and must have been sufficiently accessible to persons interested in the subject matter of its contents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Printed publication may be printed pages, electronic file, microfilm, photographs, Internet publication, photocopies. Accessibility: "distributed or otherwise made available such that persons interested and ordinarily skilled in the subject matter exercising reasonable diligence could locate it." It need not have been available to every member of the public. Issued patents and published patent applications are printed publications (as of their publication date). Disclosure must be enabling—complete enough to enable one of ordinary skill in the art to use the invention without undue experimentation; consider what would have been in the knowledge of a person of ordinary skill as of the Cutoff Date. Practice note: under pre-AIA law, instruct jury on how to determine Cutoff Date if dates of invention/priority are factual issues. Citations: 35 U.S.C. § 102(a),(b); relevant Fed. Cir. cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior Invention (Pre-AIA)
rubrics_metrics.description: [The Defendant] contends that claim ___ ... is invalid because the invention ... was invented by another person in the United States, [third party], before [§ 102(a) (pre-AIA) Cutoff Date]. That patent claim is invalid if the invention defined in that claim was invented by [third party] before [the patentee] invented his invention, [and that other person did not abandon, suppress, or conceal the invention].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: [Defendant] must show by clear and convincing evidence that (1) before [the patentee] invented his invention, [third party] reduced to practice a [product/method] that included all of the features of the claim, or (2) [third party] was first to conceive the invention and exercised reasonable diligence in later reducing the invention to practice. Prior inventor's product/method must be sufficiently developed that one skilled in the art would have recognized it would work for its intended purpose. Defense may be negated if the prior invention was abandoned, suppressed, or concealed: find that a prior inventor actively concealed the invention or unreasonably delayed making it public. Generally not abandoned if made public, sold, offered for sale, or used commercially. Periods of delay may be excused if reasonable efforts to bring to market occurred. Burden: clear and convincing. Citations: 35 U.S.C. § 102(a),(g) (pre-AIA) and cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior Patent (Pre-AIA)
rubrics_metrics.description: [The Defendant] contends that claim[s] ___ ... is invalid because the invention ... was disclosed in a patent [by [third party] before [§ 102(a) (pre-AIA) Cutoff Date]] [before [§ 102(b) (pre-AIA) Cutoff Date]]. [[That] [Those] patent claim[s] ... are invalid if the invention ... was disclosed in a patent in the United States or a foreign country [by [third party] before [§102(a) (pre-AIA) Cutoff Date]] [before §102(b) (pre-AIA) Cutoff Date].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If date of invention or priority is disputed, jury should be instructed on how to determine that date; otherwise instruct as to the Cutoff Date. Burden: defendant must prove anticipation/invalidity by clear and convincing evidence. Citations: 35 U.S.C. § 102(a),(b) (pre-AIA); relevant Fed. Cir. cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior Patent (AIA)
rubrics_metrics.description: [The Defendant] contends that claim[s] ___ ... are invalid because the claimed invention was disclosed in a patent in the United States or a foreign country before [§ 102(a) (AIA) Cutoff Date]. Patent claims are invalid if the invention was disclosed in a patent in the U.S. or foreign country before the effective filing date of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice note: if there is a factual issue whether disclosure in the patent resulted from the inventor or someone who obtained the subject matter from the inventor, the jury should be instructed on exceptions under § 102(b)(1) as needed. Identify the claimed invention's effective filing date. Citations: 35 U.S.C. §§ 102(a)(1) and (b)(1) (AIA).

rubrics_metrics.name: Earlier-Filed Patent Application (Pre-AIA) (102(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: [The Defendant] contends that claim[s] ___ ... are invalid because the invention[s] ... were described in [U.S./international PCT published patent application or patent] filed by another before [§ 102(e) (pre-AIA) Cutoff Date].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A patent claim is invalid if the invention was described in a published U.S. patent application or international PCT application published in English that designates the U.S., or a U.S. patent, filed by another person before that invention was invented by the patentee. If date of invention is disputed, instruct jury on how to determine date of invention. Citations: 35 U.S.C. §§ 102(e)(1) and (2) (pre-AIA) and cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Earlier-Filed Patent Application (AIA) (102(a)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: [The Defendant] contends that claim[s] ___ ... are invalid because the claimed invention[s] were described in [published patent document/application/patent] by another inventor that was effectively filed before [§ 102(a) (AIA) Cutoff Date] and deemed published in the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invalid if described in a published U.S. patent application, issued U.S. patent, or published international PCT application that designates the U.S., filed before the effective filing date of the claimed invention. Practice note: if factual issues exist about whether disclosure was obtained directly/indirectly from the inventor, publicly disclosed earlier by the inventor/joint inventor/another who obtained the subject matter from them, or whether the subject matter was commonly owned or subject to assignment obligations, the jury should be instructed on exceptions under §§ 102(b)(2) and (c). Determine the effective filing date per 35 U.S.C. § 102(d). Citations: 35 U.S.C. §§ 102(a)(2), (b)(2), (c), & (d); 35 U.S.C. § 374.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness—General Standard (Graham Factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: [The Defendant] contends that claim(s) ... are invalid because the claimed invention(s) would have been 'obvious.' A claimed invention is invalid as 'obvious' if it would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the art ... as of the Cutoff Date. Unlike anticipation, obviousness may be shown by considering one or more items of prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid hindsight: do not use knowledge of the patent as a road map, and do not consider what is known today. Put yourself in the place of a POSITA as of the Cutoff Date. The following factors must be evaluated for each claim: (1) scope and content of the prior art; (2) differences between the claimed invention and the prior art; (3) level of ordinary skill in the art; and (4) additional considerations (secondary considerations). Each factor must be evaluated (order flexible) and the defendant must prove obviousness by clear and convincing evidence. Obviousness is a mixed question of fact and law; consider roles of court and jury and risk of waiver by failing to move for JMOL. Citations: Graham v. John Deere; KSR; Microsoft v. i4i; relevant Fed. Cir. authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and Content of the Prior Art (First Factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: In deciding obviousness, the prior art includes the items received into evidence during the trial. A prior art reference may be considered if it discloses information designed to solve any problem or need addressed by the patent or if it discloses information that has obvious uses beyond its main purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You must decide whether the Defendant has proven by clear and convincing evidence that a specific reference is prior art. Consider whether a reference would have been reasonably examined by a POSITA when trying to solve the problem or need addressed by the patent. Practice note: if the PTO did not have all material facts, the challenger's burden may be easier to sustain; jury may be instructed to evaluate whether evidence is materially new compared to PTO consideration. Citations: Microsoft v. i4i; KSR; In re Clay; In re Wood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differences Between the Claimed Invention and the Prior Art (Second Factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze whether there are any relevant differences between the prior art and the claimed invention from the view of a person of ordinary skill in the art as of the Cutoff Date. Determine the impact of such differences on obviousness of the claimed invention as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not require precise teaching in the prior art; you may consider inferences and creative steps a POSITA would have employed. If claimed invention combined known elements and the combination yielded predictable results to a POSITA at the time, that favors obviousness. If combination yielded unexpected results or the prior art teaches away from combining elements, that favors nonobviousness. Consider whether a reason existed at the time to combine references (from prior art, background knowledge, market demand, or common sense) and whether there would have been a reasonable expectation of success. Inherency: may supply an element if it is the natural result of explicit disclosures and not shown by probabilities/possibilities; inherency must be based on the natural result and is limited in obviousness analysis. Tailor inherency instruction to evidence and give only if properly raised and supported. Citations: KSR; Graham; Arendi; PAR Pharm.; inherency cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Level of Ordinary Skill in the Art (Third Factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine obviousness, you must determine the level of ordinary skill in the field of the invention as of the Cutoff Date. The person of ordinary skill is presumed to know all prior art you have determined reasonably relevant and is a person of ordinary creativity who can use common sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If parties agree to the level, state the agreement. If not, consider evidence including: (1) level of education and experience of persons actively working in the field as of the Cutoff Date (including inventors); (2) types of problems encountered and prior art solutions as of the Cutoff Date; and (3) sophistication of the technology and rapidity of innovations as of the Cutoff Date. Citations: KSR; Graham; relevant Fed. Cir. cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary Considerations / Other Considerations (Fourth Factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider secondary considerations which may help determine whether the invention would have been obvious. No single consideration is dispositive; consider obviousness or nonobviousness of the invention as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only provide instructions on particular secondary considerations if relevant and supported by evidence and admissible (court determines admissibility and nexus). Examples include: commercial success due to the merits of the claimed invention (not advertising/promotion), long-felt but unsolved need satisfied by the invention, others tried and failed to solve the problem, others copied the invention, the invention achieved unexpectedly superior results, praise or surprise by others (including defendant), acceptance of licenses because of the merits. Patentee bears burden of proving nexus between consideration and the invention. Consider these factors along with all other evidence. Citations: Graham; U.S. v. Adams; relevant Fed. Cir. authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement Requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: [The Defendant] contends that claim(s) ___ ... are invalid for lack of enablement. [Defendant] bears the burden of establishing by clear and convincing evidence that the specification fails to satisfy the enablement requirement. A patent must disclose sufficient information to enable a person of ordinary skill in the field of the invention as of the effective filing date to make and use the full scope of the claimed invention without undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enablement is a question of law for the Court; jury may be instructed on subsidiary fact issues only if specific factual issues bearing on enablement are to be decided by the jury. Patents are written for persons of ordinary skill; a patent need not state information that such a person would be likely to know. Some experimentation does not defeat enablement; consider Wands factors (non-exhaustive) including: quantity of experimentation necessary and whether it involves known/common techniques; amount of direction or guidance in the patent; presence/absence of working examples; nature of the invention; state of the prior art; relative skill of those in the art; predictability of the art; breadth of the claims. Burden: clear and convincing. Citations: 35 U.S.C. § 112; Amgen v. Sanofi; In re Wands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written-Description Requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: [The Defendant] contends that claim(s) ___ ... are invalid for failure to satisfy the written-description requirement. [Defendant] bears the burden of establishing by clear and convincing evidence that the specification fails to satisfy the written-description requirement. A patent must contain a written description of the product/method claimed in the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Written-description ensures the applicant actually invented the claimed subject matter. To satisfy it, the specification must describe each and every limitation of a claim with clear, concise, and exact terms. However, exact words need not be used; specific examples are not required. The specification must show that a person of ordinary skill would recognize that the inventor possessed the claimed subject matter as of the effective filing date. Evaluate sufficiency claim-by-claim. Factors to consider: nature and scope of claims; complexity, predictability, and maturity of technology; existing knowledge in the field; scope and content of prior art. Burden: clear and convincing. Citations: 35 U.S.C. § 112; Ariad; other Fed. Cir. cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages—General Principles
rubrics_metrics.description: If you find that the accused device/method infringes any asserted claim and those claims are not invalid, you must determine the type and amount of damages to be awarded the Plaintiff. The Plaintiff must prove each element of its damages—including the amount—by a preponderance of the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Damages must be adequate to compensate the Plaintiff for the infringement, putting the Plaintiff in about the same financial position it would have been in absent the infringement. Damages cannot be punitive and may not include interest or other add-ons. The minimum measure is a reasonable royalty. Consider damages only if you find one or more asserted claims both not invalid and infringed. Citations: 35 U.S.C. § 284; WesternGeco; ResQNet; other cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Date Damages Begin / Notice and Marking (Alternate Rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: 10.1.1 Alternate A: if parties stipulate, the start date for damages is the stipulated date. 10.1.2 Alternate B: if disputed, the date damages begin is the date Plaintiff first notified Defendant of its claim for patent infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two ways to give notice: (1) Public notice by marking substantially all products that include the patented invention with the patent number (or 'Patent'/'Pat' and a freely accessible Internet address tying product to patent), including licensees who use the patented invention—marking must be substantially all products in a consistent and continuous manner. Public marking is effective even if defendant did not see it. (2) Direct notice: specifically notify defendant of alleged infringement; effective as of the date defendant received notice. Plaintiff must prove by preponderance that defendant was put on notice as of the date alleged. If Plaintiff did not provide effective notice prior to filing suit, consequences follow (instruction continues beyond chunk).
